# Proverbs 1 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A)

---

**1** These are the proverbs of Solomon — David's son, Israel's king:

**2** Written so you can learn what wisdom and discipline are all about, and understand words that bring real insight,

**3** So you can learn to live with good sense — doing what is right, just, and fair,

**4** So that those who lack experience can gain shrewdness, and the young can find knowledge and direction.

**5** Even the wise should listen and learn more, and those with understanding will discover how to navigate life,

**6** Learning to interpret proverbs, parables, the sayings of the wise, and their puzzling questions.

**7** Reverence for the LORD is where knowledge begins; only fools reject wisdom and refuse to learn.

**8** Listen, my child, to what your father teaches you, and don't walk away from what your mother has shown you,

**9** Because their words will crown your life with grace and adorn you like a fine necklace.

**10** My child, when people who do wrong try to pull you in, don't go along with it.

**11** When they say, 'Come on, let's set a trap for someone — let's ambush some innocent person just for the thrill of it,

**12** We'll swallow them whole like the grave takes the dead, like those who vanish into the pit,

**13** We'll grab every kind of valuable thing and stuff our houses full of stolen goods,

**14** Throw in your lot with us — we'll split everything equally' —

**15** My child, don't take a single step down that road. Stay far away from their path,

**16** Because they are running headlong toward violence; they can't wait to spill blood.

**17** It's pointless to set a trap in plain sight of a bird,

**18** Yet these people are setting a trap for themselves — they're risking their own lives.

**19** This is what happens to everyone driven by greed — it ends up consuming the very person who pursues it.

**20** Meanwhile, Wisdom stands in the open street, calling out. She raises her voice in the public squares,

**21** She shouts above the noise of the crowd; at the city gates she makes her appeal:

**22** "How long will you naive people cling to your ignorance? How long will cynics enjoy their cynicism and fools resist learning?

**23** Come back when I correct you! Look — I'm ready to pour out my thoughts to you and share everything I know.

**24** But I've been calling out to you, and you've refused to listen. I've been reaching out, and you haven't paid any attention.

**25** You've brushed aside everything I've said, and you haven't wanted any part of my correction —

**26** So when disaster hits you, I'll be the one laughing. When what you dread comes crashing in, I won't hold back my scorn,

**27** When your worst fears arrive like a violent storm, when trouble and pain overwhelm you.

**28** Then you'll call for me — but I won't answer. You'll search desperately for me, but you won't find me,

**29** Because you turned your back on knowledge and refused to respect the LORD,

**30** Because you rejected my guidance and dismissed every warning I gave.

**31** So you'll eat the bitter fruit of the choices you made, and choke on the consequences of your own schemes.

**32** The stubbornness of the naive will be their death, and the self-satisfaction of fools will be their ruin;

**33** But whoever pays attention to me will live in safety, completely at peace, with nothing to fear."

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

- **1:7**: This is the thesis statement of the entire book — everything else builds on this foundation. 'Fear' here doesn't mean terror; it means recognizing who God is.

- **1:20-21**: Wisdom is imagined as a woman shouting in the streets — a bold, public figure, not a quiet scholar in a library. She's impossible to ignore.

- **1:32-33**: The contrast is sharp and intentional: the naive are destroyed by their own stubbornness, but those who listen live without fear.

— PNEUMA
